Inspired by the cut-up technique by William S. Burroughs, which was later used by David Bowie to create some of his song lyrics.

It generates a sequential list of a few hundred words that are placed at random locations on the canvas without overlapping.

Under the hood, a home-built spatial subdivision algorithm is used to look for empty spaces where the next random word might fit.

Originally, the plan was to publish this work with categorized words that somehow fit together into a theme, but after playing around with it, I found that this didn't match the original idea of the cut-up technique.
Also, it was very interesting to see completely arbitrary and unrelated words close together, forming incomplete fragments of a possible sentence. Just use your imagination!

The list of words was created while thinking about the current situation in the world and reading the news. Note, however, that it may happen that some words close to each other form a strange combination.

"AN2: Recuerdos" is an abstract collection that is the direct sequel to Artificialmente Natural. Recuerdos are memories in Spanish, and with this collection, I tried to evoke specifically that, a memory. There are many times throughout our life that our memory changes and grow. Sometimes we even alter memories unconsciously, mixing them up between other memories and even fantasy or dreams (ever had a Deja Vu?), creating a new memory solely based on an idea of the past and what it was. We live in a world of perceptions, and that is exactly what our memory is, a combination of perceptions that became ideas, made up of other older ideas and new ones, to then get stored inside our brain as new memories.

Now, you may ask, cool story, but what does it have to do with the collection? Well, through your memories, experiences, and perceptions, you're going to analyze the piece. You may think you see an abstract ocean in the background, or a sky, or waves, or auras. You may feel that the art piece sometimes looks decayed, splattered with paint, or just splattered with dirty noise. The truth is that through your memory, you're going to try to make sense of it no matter if you like what you're seeing or not, and that's the sole idea of everything. Interpreting through our experiences is how we calm the tension we feel from the unknown. You can't make a comparison or an interpretation if you haven't seen or experienced something that laid an idea inside your brain, becoming multiple other ideas through plasticity and neural connectivity, always trying to make sense of everything. That's why your "recuerdos" is the key to the way you interpret life and live it, both unconsciously and consciously. 

For me, this collection consciously reminds me of my teenage years. A little chaotic at times, with some beautiful moments of self-discovery. Mistakes were made, love was found and lost, and everything was pretty colorful and new. Unconsciously, I don't know, that's the beauty of the unknown.

17320.d:
Limina is a study of the fine line between order and chaos.

Each piece of the collection is made up of just one or two lines. These lines are defined by thousands of points that are chosen, one by one, by a simple algorithm moving across the canvas. What arises from that simple concept is a surprising variety of intricate patterns, accidental symmetries and traces of order in chaotic structures. 

Limina is a meditation on the concept of emergence, a concept that lies at the heart of generative art. The algorithm that defines the core of the series is only capable of making one simple choice: left, right, up or down? As it moves across the canvas, it leaves a trace of points that are connected by a curve. The order in which these points are chosen and the tightness of the curve connecting them is what creates the visual diversity of Limina. As these values fluctuate, symmetries emerge and break down again, forms, patterns and ornaments are created and combined to form both complex structures and simple abstractions. 

Limina shows the potential of minimalist generative concepts to generate visually dense and unexpected results.

17322.d:
Neurons are responsible for carrying information throughout the human body. Using electrical and chemical signals, they help coordinate all of the necessary functions of life. In this article, we explain what neurons are and how they work.

In short, our nervous systems detect what is going on around us and inside of us; they decide how we should act, alter the state of internal organs (heart rate changes, for instance), and allows us to think about and remember what is going on. To do this, it relies on a sophisticated network — neurons.

Neurons can only be seen using a microscope and can be split into three parts:

Soma (cell body) — this portion of the neuron receives information. It contains the cell’s nucleus.

Dendrites — these thin filaments carry information from other neurons to the soma. They are the “input” part of the cell.

Axon — this long projection carries information from the soma and sends it off to other cells. This is the “output” part of the cell. It normally ends with a number of synapses connecting to the dendrites of other neurons.

Both dendrites and axons are sometimes referred to as nerve fibers.

This work is a tribute to Victor Vasarely. 

The algorithm reproduces part of the visual grammar of certain works by the artist and extends the resources used in his works by incorporating new elements. Each work is defined by the superposition of 2 or 3 layers made up of a grid of figures: squares, circles or triangles, each of which can be filled or hollow. 

Each layer has an evolution gradient that affects its color, and that can also affect other parameters of the figures in the grid, such as size, transparency, rotation or displacement. There are at least 8 different types of gradients that can affect each of these parameters.

At the same time, each layer can be affected by a subdivision into sectors that make changes to shapes, gradients, colors and the rest of the parameters. These subdivisions can be in the form of checkerboards, in either vertical or horizontal halves, or within an internal section.

This is an algorithmic tribute to the pioneering work of Anna Atkins (1799-1871). Considered by many the first female photographer, Atkins learned about the cyanotype process soon after it was invented by John Herschel, a family friend. As a botanist, she had the idea of using the new technique to produce contact prints of plants. Her investigations succeeded in capturing the nuances in morphology and the delicate details of many species.

In 1843 she published “British Algae: Cyanotype impressions”, the first published book to use a photographic process for the illustrations. Each copy gathered around 400 prints, each of them individually produced from a different specimen. Thus, all books featured the same species, but each of them was different, in a process that was itself generative in a certain way. Today, about 17 copies of the book are preserved in different institutions. Atkins went on to publish two more books in the following years, with the help of her friend Anne Dixon, dedicated to various ferns and plants.

“Cyanotypes” pays homage to her wonderful work, which sits at the intersection between science and art, and used technology in a novel way to capture the beauty of nature. Here things are taken one step forward, to generate algorithmic simulations of plants, ferns, and algae, which are the work of fantasy and not necessarily faithful to the traits of any real species.

The work features 28 basic configurations, each of them in turn capable of unlimited variations. As was the case with the prints from “British Algae”, every image is at the same time part of a series and unique.

This is the second in series of works where we pay homage to Ken Knowlton, scientist and computer graphic pioneer and artist who passed on June 16, 2022. Ken Knowlton developed the famous EXPLOR language, (Explicit 2-D Patterns, Local Operations, and Randomness) while at Bell Labs. He published a paper describing it in 1975 entitled: MINI-EXPLOR, A FORTRAN-Coded Version of the EXPLOR Language for Mini (and larger) Computers. (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/988049.988052)

This work is a mark of progress. Christopher Scussel and I are working on modernizing MINI-EXPLOR. Chris is working on updating the engine from the original FORTRAN code of the 1970’s and its other limitations to usable JavaScript. In concert, I am analyzing and synthesizing the capabilities of the code and identifying an aesthetic. Together we continue to update EXPLOR and add new features.

CPoSOP Composition is an original derivative work of Contour Plot of Superimposed Octagonal Pyramids that was one of Knowlton’s original test examples. (Example 3)

The original EXPLOR picture frame was limited to a fixed array of 140 x 140 “characters.” Chris has rewritten the code to make the picture space variable. In this piece I increased the image space to a resolution 250 x 250  picture cells. Each picture cell is a 3x3 pixel block. 

The EXPLOR functions are designed to interact with the current contents of each cell in the picture array. Every EXPLOR function has a rules parameter. In this test I’ve added a background. Thus when I draw my modified CPoSOP widget over the background it interacts with the color contents of a background cell or, the color of the cell based on a previously drawn widget.

I’ve modified the original CPoSOP code and replaced constants with random variables. (made it a Spatial Force). I create a regular grid (Form of Spatial Organization) of a random size and draw the CPoSOP widget 85% of the time in one of the grid elements positions. The grid provides a structure to the image and the CPoSOP widget provides visual interest. The interaction of the widgets with the background and each other are amazing. 

In keeping true to an EXPLOR vibe we use 4 color palettes. We let the computer randomly pick from three predefined palettes: Black and white. Four colors randomly chosen from set of 8 “Bauhaus” colors. And, four truly random colors.
